summary: Provides PCEP extensions to support Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA) in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks. Besides routing, such networks must decide which wavelength to use on each hop of a path.

eli5.summary: In a fibre network each light colour is like a lane. This lets a route planner pick the path and the colour for each part.

questions: how does pcep handle wavelength assignment
what is the wa object in pcep
subtitle: How a path computation client asks a PCE for a route and the wavelength to use on each hop of an optical path.

tldr.problem: In a wavelength switched optical network, finding a route is not enough: the path also needs a wavelength on each hop, and PCEP had no way to ask for or return one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Wavelength Assignment (WA) object with TLVs for wavelength selection and restrictions, a Wavelength Allocation TLV in the reply, signal-compatibility restrictions, and new error and no-path codes.
tldr.outcome: A single PCE can now compute route and wavelength together, returning either explicit labels or a label set. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8780 is a Proposed Standard, and it is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Routing Plus Wavelength Assignment
sections.content:
A Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON) is a WDM-based optical network where switching is done by the wavelength of an optical signal. Setting up a path in one needs Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA): besides the route, the network must decide which wavelength is used on each hop. The RFC treats wavelength assignment as an additional routing constraint.

Two rules shape the problem. Two optical channels that share a fibre link cannot use the same wavelength, or they would interfere. And where a node cannot convert wavelengths, the whole optical path should use the same wavelength on every link, the wavelength-continuity constraint. Nodes that can convert wavelengths, such as 3R regenerators, relax that constraint, but the RFC notes such converters can be limited by their relatively high cost.

This document extends PCEP (RFC 5440) to carry these requests, based on the requirements in RFC 6163 and RFC 7449. It does not address optical impairments.
sections.eli5: Imagine several trains sharing one tunnel, each needing its own coloured lane. Planning the trip means choosing the stations and also the lane colour, and two trains in the same tunnel cannot use the same colour.

sections.title: The Combined Process Architecture
sections.content:
The extensions assume the Combined Process (R&WA) architecture from RFC 6163, where a single PCE does both the routing and the wavelength assignment. The PCC (the client, which may be an optical switching element) sends one request and gets back a route with wavelengths.

The PCE can deliver the wavelength in two ways. With Explicit Label Control it picks the label to use on each interface or node along the path. With a Label Set it gives each node a range of candidate labels, so that the actual allocation is finished by distributed signaling. When a range is offered, a request SHOULD say which heuristic should be used for the choice.
sections.eli5: One helper plans both the road and the lane colour in a single go. The helper can either say exactly which colour for each stretch, or hand over a list of allowed colours and let each stop choose.

sections.title: The WA Object and Its TLVs
sections.content:
A request carries a new Wavelength Assignment (WA) object, Object-Class 42, Object-Type 1. In a PCReq it MUST come after the END-POINTS object, and it is mandatory for these requests. Its body has 16 reserved bits, a 16-bit flags field with one defined flag, and TLVs, at least one of which MUST be present.

The M flag sets the allocation mode. When it is 1, the label from the PCE must be explicit, using Explicit Label Control on each hop. When it is 0, the PCE may suggest labels as a Label Set to allow distributed assignment, and it MUST return a Label Set field in the response.

Two TLVs are defined for the object:

  • Wavelength Selection (type 8, fixed length of 32 bits) says in what order wavelengths should be chosen. It applies only when M is set and MUST NOT be used when it is clear. Its encoding comes from RFC 7689.
  • Wavelength Restriction (type 9, variable length) limits which wavelengths may be used.
sections.eli5: The request gets a special form. One tick box says whether you want exact colours or just a list of options, and extra notes can say how to pick a colour and which colours are off limits.

sections.title: Wavelength Restrictions
sections.content:
For any request that includes wavelength assignment, the PCC MUST specify a restriction on the wavelengths to use. The PCE reads it as a constraint on the tuning ability of the origin laser transmitter or as another maintenance-related limit. The PCC can add constraints even when the PCE already knows the transmitter's tunability.

The Wavelength Restriction TLV is a repeatable group of an Action (8 bits), a Count (8 bits), 16 reserved bits, one or more link identifiers and a wavelength constraint. Action 0 is an inclusive list of links and action 1 is an inclusive range, which takes exactly two identifiers where a zero means no bound. Values 2 to 255 are unassigned. Links are assumed to be bidirectional. A Count of zero applies the wavelength restriction to all links, and all identifiers in one list MUST be of the same type.

A link identifier has a type: 1 for an IPv4 address, 2 for an IPv6 address and 3 for an unnumbered interface (a 4-byte TE node ID plus a 4-byte interface ID). The wavelength constraint is a Label Set field from RFC 7579 with an LSC label from RFC 6205, with actions for inclusive or exclusive lists, inclusive or exclusive ranges and bitmap sets.
sections.eli5: Along with the request you can say which colours your equipment can make, and for which stretches of the trip. You can name a stretch by its address, or say the rule fits every stretch.

sections.title: Signal Compatibility Restrictions
sections.content:
The sender and receiver of an optical path must have matching signal processing capabilities, such as modulation and Forward Error Correction, expressed through the Optical Interface Class (OIC). Path computation therefore checks the capabilities at each interface, and the PCE MUST have a way to learn them, for example from the TED through an IGP or an NMS.

Two new TLVs carry these restrictions as endpoint restrictions in the generalized END-POINTS object: the Optical Interface Class List TLV (type 11) and the Client Signal Information TLV (type 12). Their value encodings come from RFC 7581. Bit rate is already covered by the BANDWIDTH object.

The PCC or PCE can also exclude or include a kind of signal processing along the path. For the Exclude Route Object (RFC 5521) the RFC adds subobject type 8 for the Optical Interface Class List and type 9 for Client Signal Information. For the Include Route Object the same two types 8 and 9 are added, with the L field in place of X. The only permitted Attribute values are 0 (Interface) and 1 (Node).
sections.eli5: The two ends of the fibre have to speak the same light language. The request can list which languages are fine, or which ones must not appear anywhere on the route.

sections.title: The Reply: Allocation and Failures
sections.content:
The reply carries a Wavelength Allocation TLV (type 10), with a flags field whose M bit is 0 when the allocation relies on Label Sets and 1 when it uses Explicit Label Control. It lists link identifiers and the allocated wavelengths, using the same encodings as the request. It rides in a PCRep as an Attribute TLV in the Hop Attribute subobjects of the Explicit Route Object.

The RFC defines Error-Type 27 (WSON RWA Error). Value 1 means the PCE lacks memory to process the request, value 2 means it cannot compute RWA, and value 3 means a syntactical encoding error such as an unknown Action value or the wrong number of identifiers in a range. In the first two cases the PCE stops processing and the request is cancelled at the PCC.

If no route is found, the NO-PATH object can carry a NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV. Bit 23 tells the PCC that no feasible route met all the RWA constraints, such as wavelength restriction and signal compatibility.
sections.eli5: The answer lists each stretch with its colour, or a list of allowed colours. If the planner cannot help, it answers with a numbered reason, such as being out of memory, not knowing how to plan colours, or not understanding the form.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The RFC says the security considerations of RFC 5440 apply and that it introduces no new security issues. If an operator wants to keep the WSON information private, PCEPS (TLS for PCEP, RFC 8253) SHOULD be used.

For manageability, a PCEP implementation SHOULD let the operator configure whether a PCC can send WSON RWA requests and whether a PCE supports them, plus WSON-RWA-specific policies such as authorized senders and a request rate limiter. No new liveness, verification or network-operation requirements are added beyond those in RFC 5440.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is dangerous here, but if the map of your network is private, use the locked version of the connection. Operators can also choose who may ask and how often.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS THE PCE HANDS OVER A WAVELENGTH

items.title: Explicit Label Control
items.text: The PCE picks the label for each interface or node along the path. M bit is 1.

items.title: Label Set
items.text: The PCE gives a range of labels and the nodes finish allocation during signaling. M bit is 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use; SHOULD be zeroed and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Holds the M bit (Wavelength Allocation Mode) in its last bit.

items.label: Insufficient memory
items.desc: The PCE cannot process the RWA request; the request is cancelled at the PCC.

items.label: RWA computation not supported
items.desc: The PCE is not capable of RWA computation.

items.label: Syntactical encoding error
items.desc: For example an unknown Action value, unknown identifier type or no matching link.
